chapter_theme: Civakan's companions ride out with a caravan, after reading the omens, through hill and field country to a hermitage, where they find a weeping woman ascetic worshipping the Jina; she is Vijayai, his mother, though no one names her, and when she will not tell her clan Devadattan answers with their city, their parents and their upbringing with the prince, and begins to tell his deeds.

cast.role: Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother, living as an ascetic in the hermitage; unnamed in these verses
Civakan's companions, here the four who ride out and meet Vijayai without knowing her
the caravan and armed escort travelling with the companions
the men skilled in reading day, omens and hour who fix the departure
one of Civakan's companions, son of Vijayadattan and Piritimati, who speaks for the party
the hero, absent, whose deeds Devadattan recounts

1773.reading: The narrator lists the party's train, trained horses, swift chariots and fierce camels, beasts that cover a hundred bow-lengths in a snap of the fingers, loaded with the goods they took.
1773.event: The companions' train is made ready with mounts and loaded goods.
1773.nuance: ஒட்டகம், the camel, is a rare beast in this landscape; the verse piles up speed (நொடிப்பின் மாத்திரை நூற்றுவில்) rather than describing any one animal.

1774.reading: Four horses, swift of foot, coloured like the green parrot, with coral-like hooves and eye-catching looks, worth the price of the world, are saddled and the four mount them.
1774.event: The four companions mount four saddled horses.

1775.reading: Having had men skilled in the art examine the day, the bird omen, the good standing of the planets, the hour and the signs, they set out with the caravan, urging on with their feet.
1775.nuance: Five separate reckonings are named (நாள், புள், கோள், ஓரை, நிமித்தம) and handed to specialists (ஆளும் மாந்தர்); the verse records the practice without saying it decides the outcome.
1775.event: The companions have the day, omens and hour read and set out with the caravan.

1776.reading: With drums and conches roaring all round, sheathed swords and bright spears flashing, the army sets out with a shout like red flood water that has broken its dam.
1776.event: The armed escort sets out noisily.

1777.reading: Along the way jasmine flowers shower onto the bent ears of ripe red paddy, and the swans and herons of the flooded fields scatter as the drums sound.

1778.reading: Elephants with winnow-like ears and hanging trunks, set swaying in the pepper forest where hens and cocks play under areca clusters and pepper vines swing, take fright and bolt.
1778.nuance: The swing (ஊசல்) of pepper vines and the play of fowl are the settled hill country; the party's noise, not a hunt, is what startles the elephants (இளகப் பரிகொண்ட).

1779.reading: Passing hills with waterfalls, dark-forested slopes, millet fields where sparrows rise crying, and the lands of those who have lost their fortune, the train comes and halts within the hermitage of the great ascetics.
1779.nuance: திருவிற் றீர்ந்தவர் தேயம், 'the land of those parted from fortune', is set just before the hermitage where Vijayai, who lost her kingdom, lives; the poet lets the phrase stand ahead of the meeting.
1779.event: The train passes through hill and field country and halts at a hermitage.

1780.reading: The grove there, where bees sleep, cuckoos call and peacocks cry, where many flowers open and drip honey, branches bend under tender leaves and buds, is like the world of the gods.

1781.reading: Among pools full of kaavi, kazhuneer, kuvalai, aambal and fragrant lotus, with young herons, paired swans, old fish and bees, the people make camp between the tanks and the grove.
1781.event: The party camps between the pools and the grove of the hermitage.

1782.reading: In the hermitage where the ascetics dwell, the young men wander everywhere and, on a cool wooden bench in a bower of plucked flowers, they see a woman a little beyond Lakshmi herself.
1782.nuance: The woman is Vijayai, Civakan's mother, though neither the verse nor the young men name her; the reader knows from 347-359 who lives in this hermitage. செய்யவள் is Lakshmi, and the line places her above the goddess even in her ascetic state.
1782.event: The companions, wandering the hermitage, see a woman seated on a wooden bench.

1783.reading: Her fine ochre-dyed cloth weighs on her hips, the fine red upper cloth weighs on her shoulder where it covers it, her little dark-haired son weighs on her mind, and her eyes, as if plucking at her, weigh on her as she weeps unable to bear it.
1783.nuance: The four-fold வருத்த joins the ascetic's garments and the son in one list of burdens: the robe she took for him has not freed her from him. The 'little son' (சிறுவன்) is grown by now; she still thinks of him as the infant she left.
1783.event: The woman sits in her ascetic's dress weeping for her son.

1784.reading: Her five-plaited hair, dimmed with dirt and like threaded sapphire, hangs down her back unanointed and bound by its own neglect; laying fragrant flowers on the feet of the Jina in a hidden place, she recites praises in her mind that her fault may go, and sits worshipping.
1784.nuance: வாமன் here is the Jina, the one whose feet receive the flowers; the worship is silent (மனத்து ஓதி) and private (மறைந்த வழி). The hair 'not anointed' (பூசுதலும் இன்றி) is the widow's mark of 349-354, kept now as a penance.
1784.event: The woman worships at the feet of the Jina, reciting praises silently.

claims.claim: praise and flowers at the Jina's feet remove one's fault

1785.reading: Saying 'I will think now on my son's lot', she sits there while tears run from her long eyes and wet the cloth over her breasts; the young men come up to her, their hearts trembling, and bow with joy and great love.
1785.nuance: Her thought for her son comes straight after the worship of 1784: the prayer does not end the grief but leads into it. The companions bow with love to a stranger; the reader alone knows she is their prince's mother.
1785.event: The woman weeps thinking of her son, and the young men approach and bow to her.

1786.reading: Seeing her dwelling in the hermitage girt by hills, they cannot tell whether she is the goddess with spear-long eyes who lives in the fragrant flower, the bright-browed goddess who lives on the tongue clothed in speech, or the sweet-voiced one clothed by the waves.
1786.nuance: The three are Lakshmi of the lotus, Sarasvati of the tongue, and a third named only as clothed in waves (திரையுடுத்த), perhaps the sea-girt earth; the triple உடுத்த ('clothed') ties the three together.
1786.event: The young men wonder which goddess she is.

1787.reading: The young men ask her, 'You who are like the great goddess of fortune whose auspiciousness has died, what brings you here, and what is the lady's clan?', and she answers that her clan and her coming are not easy to tell if they would know them, and bids them tell their own clan and coming first.
1787.nuance: Lines 1-2 are the young men's question and lines 3-4 her reply. மங்கலம் மடிந்த, 'whose auspiciousness has died', reads her as a widow from her dress. Her refusal keeps the secret of land and lineage the deity kept for her when she came (356).
1787.event: The young men ask the woman her clan; she declines and asks theirs.

1788.reading: Devadattan answers that their dwelling place is the city of Rajamapuram, famed for its watchfulness, where young vaalai fish crowding the old deep water sleep after fighting with the bow-shaped prawns.
1788.nuance: The speaker of 1788-1796 is fixed only by 1792, where he names himself.
1788.event: Devadattan names Rajamapuram as their city.

1789.reading: He names the first of them: Sitattan, lion-like, with shoulders that make kings tremble, son of Kurudattai of long sword-like eyes, the wife worthy of Sagaran, the golden-chested minister of subtle understanding.
1789.nuance: Each companion in 1789-1792 is named through both parents, the mother's beauty and the father's office or skill, so that the list is a list of lineages answering her question about clan. The father here is a minister (மந்திரி); whether this Sitattan is the merchant Sitattan of the sea voyage (493-580) the verses do not settle.

1790.reading: Next is Buddhisenan, son of Achalan, master of the four Vedas beyond measure, and of Tilottamai, whose beauty matches the goddess of fortune; his chest is like a hill, and Devadattan says he would tire if he told his splendour.
1790.nuance: Buddhisenan's father is a man of the four Vedas (நான்மறையினான்); the companions are of mixed birth, brahmin, minister's and merchant's sons, joined only by having been born on one day. Line 3 (விளைத்திரும்பு மேய்ந்தொழிந்த மிச்சில்) is obscure as divided.

1791.reading: Then Padumukan, born to Pavittirai of bright brow and angry sword-like eyes, wife of the merchant Danapalan, whose honeyed chest bears the scars a musth elephant ploughed with its tusk.

1792.reading: Last he names himself: 'I, sir, am Devadattan, the loving son of Piritimati of unmatched chastity, who is the life's armour of Vijayadattan of bow-scarred shoulders, who won an emblem bearing the king's name in the golden city.'
1792.nuance: His mother is called the 'life's armour' (உயிர்க் கவசம்) of his father, chastity praised as a protection to the husband, said to a woman who has outlived hers.
1792.event: Devadattan names himself and his parents.

1793.reading: He says that on the very day the king perished through their own ill deeds, they were born together with their prince, who is their life; they were given to the prince as his companions, and grew like the sun in beauty.
1793.nuance: எங்கள் வினையால் takes the king's death as the companions' own karma, a humble formula the epic gives to several dependants (the deity as maid in 315). He tells this to the king's widow without knowing her.
1793.event: Devadattan tells how the companions were born on the day of the king's death and given to the prince.

claims.claim: a master's fall can be the fruit of his dependants' own deeds

1794.reading: When years had passed, Nandattan, the prince's younger brother, with Nabulan and Vipulan of noble qualities, grew up with them and reached the height of the raised seat, like the elephants of the quarters, with a heat none could touch.
1794.nuance: Line 4 (தீண்டரிய வெம்மையொடு திக்கயங்கள் எனவே) ends the sentence on a simile without a main verb; the next verse completes the account.

1795.reading: They all learned together archery, swordplay, the contest of the vina, wrestling, the work of the hide shield, the handling of elephants and the fine art of the horse, swimming across all the arts.
1795.nuance: The vina is listed among the martial arts as a contest (வீணைபொரு தொழில்), which is how Civakan used it to win Gandharvadattai.

1796.reading: And if she asks the name of the prince who rescued the herds from the hunters of cruel bows, won by vina contest the daughter of the Vidyadhara king who goes back to the sky, overcame the elephant and enjoyed Gunamalai's love, it is this.
1796.nuance: Devadattan recounts Civakan's deeds in order (the cattle raid, the vina contest, the elephant and Gunamalai) to the one listener who most needs them and who has not yet been told whose they are; the name itself is held over to the next verse.

links.note: The ochre-dyed fine cloth (கல் தோய் நுண் கலிங்கம், 353; நுண்டுகில் கல்லரத்தம், 1783) that Vijayai put on 'that the strong one's son may rise'.
links.teaches: The robe she took as a vow for her son's rise is still on her years later and is now listed beside the son as a burden, so the renunciation proves to have been made for him rather than from him.

links.note: In 359 she watches the road for news of her son; in 1785 she still sits thinking of his lot when the news walks in.
links.teaches: The waiting begun in 359 is answered not by her messenger but by strangers who stumble on her, so the news she longed for comes unsought and unrecognised.

links.note: In 356 the deity hid her land and lineage when commending her to the ascetics; here she herself refuses to tell her clan.
links.teaches: The concealment first done for her by the deity has become her own habit, so that she withholds her identity even from her son's companions and the recognition must wait on their story.

links.note: 785 says the companions were born on the very day Civakan was born; 1793 says that day was also the day the king perished, through their own deeds.
links.teaches: The birthday the battle verse gave as a warrior's pedigree is retold to the king's widow as a day of death, and the companions take the guilt of it on themselves.

links.note: In 334 Vijayai heard her son's future greatness foretold; in 1796 his first deeds are recited to her by one who does not know she is his mother.
links.teaches: The prophecy she took on faith returns to her as report of deeds done, and the irony that the reciter does not know his listener lets the mother hear her son's fame as a stranger would.

links.note: The couplet promises that those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere; Vijayai worships at the Jina's feet and in the next verse weeps for her son.
links.teaches: Placed beside the couplet, the scene shows worship at the passionless one's feet asked to remove a fault while the grief of attachment to a child runs on, so the promised freedom from suffering is a goal still far off, not a present state.

gains.a: the epic's silent worship gains a standard, the couplet's 'no suffering at any time', against which her tears in 1785 read as the distance still to go
gains.b: the couplet gains a case of a worshipper at the right feet whose suffering persists, which tests whether 'reaching' the feet means worship or attainment

links.note: The Puram queen refuses to be one of the widows who go unanointed, eat cooked leaves and sleep on gravel, and chooses the pyre; Vijayai lives that very widow's life, unanointed, on greens (354), as a Jain ascetic.
links.teaches: The life the Sangam queen scorns as the wretched alternative to the pyre is the one the Jain epic gives its queen as a penance lived for a son, so the two show the widow's choice valued in opposite ways.

gains.a: the epic's unanointed ascetic gains the older measure by which her survival was the lesser choice, sharpening why she lives on: for her son
gains.b: the Puram poem gains a widow who takes the 'leaf-food' life deliberately and turns it into austerity, a reply its speaker does not imagine

new_concepts.gloss: an omen or sign read as foretelling what will come
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: கொண்ட நிமித்தமும் (1775, line 2)

source_issues: 1782 lines 1-2 (மாண்டிழகர், செய்கழகர் தாரரவர்) are divided obscurely; the reading 'young men' for the subject is a guess from context.
1790 line 3 (விளைத்திரும்பு மேய்ந்தொழிந்த மிச்சில்வரை மார்பன்) is obscure as divided.
1794 line 4 ends without a main verb; the construction runs on into 1795.
1796 ends with the name withheld (நாமம் எவன் என்னின் இது ஆம்); the name follows in 1797.
